newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Klima flush with offers as CA tender closes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Klima flush with offers as CA tender closes.

text.p: With three firm offers for privatisation candidate Creditanstalt under his belt, Austrian Finance Minister Viktor Klima on Monday predicted he would have no trouble picking a winner before year-end.

Barely two weeks ago, the minister had a lone bid for the state's 70 percent voting stake in the flagship bank. This time around, Klima seems spoilt for choice and analysts cautioned he would have to weigh his options carefully.

Retail king Karl Wlaschek, his pockets brimming with around 15 billion schillings ($1.4 billion) in cash from the sale of his Billa supermarket empire in July, emerged as a mystery contender in the battle for control of Creditanstalt, the country's blue-blooded bank.

Meanwhile, Swiss heavyweight UBS strengthened a long-standing group of bidders led by insurer EA-Generali, enabling it to reach for the government's entire stake with a view to placing parts of it on the market.
Market leader Bank Austria, which caused a storm in Vienna's placid financial scene last week when it unveiled its own bid, also submitted a firm offer ahead of the 0700 GMT deadline.

"We will now carefully evaluate all the bids in order to find the best possible solution," Klima said, delighted by the prospect of a windfall for his leaking state budget. "We will make a decision before the end of the year."
At current market prices, the state's 19.9 million ordinary shares in Creditanstalt are worth some 14.5 billion schillings. But Klima is clearly hoping for more than that.
Bank Austria is reported to be willing to spend around 16 billion schillings for control of its fiercest rival, erstwhile banker for the Austro-Hungarian emperors.

But the offer is fraught with political pitfalls -- Bank Austria is a bastion of the ruling Social Democrats, while Creditanstalt is firmly seated in the camp of the conservative People's Party, the Social Democrat's junior coalition partner.

Prompted by Bank Austria's offer, the conservative-backed EA-Generali consortium, which includes Germany's Commerzbank, Banca Commerciale Italiana and Austrian savings bank Die Erste, quickly boosted its own bid and secured UBS's help to find the extra cash it needed.
The "core consortium" would buy 74 percent of the state's stake, while a second group would take on the remaining shares and place them on the market later, with UBS acting as global coordinator.
"UBS is part of the placement consortium and will not be involved in a possible long-term solution," said EA-Generali spokesman Josef Hlinka.

Analysts said 79-year old Wlaschek's surprise foray into the world of international banking was little more than a sidebar to what has become Austria's longest-running privatisation project but welcomed the consortium's beefed-up bid and forecast a closely fought contest with Bank Austria.
"The government is unlikely to sell to a private individual," said Victoria Maxwell at James Capel in London.
"Between them the members of the consortium have the money and they can keep pushing up their bid and give Bank Austria a run for its money," she said.

Another London-based analyst agreed Bank Austria's bid, if successful, offered the best hope for a reform of the country's overcrowded banking system but said synergies might be difficult to realise in a country where political and economic might was divided carefully along party lines.
"(That scenario) certainly has the most potential but whether that potential will be realised is the question," he said.
